title: Bilateral targets shared fewer sites than fixed-count control means in eight worm brain maps
abstract: We tested whether left-right partner neurons share chemical synaptic sites more often than source-target contact counts predict. Eight public C. elegans brain maps supplied site membership in a fixed 162-cell panel. Controls kept each source-target count and each site target count. The observed bilateral shared-site totals were 0.717 to 0.915 times the control means. This was opposite to the proposed enrichment. Equal weighting of eligible source-pairs did not give the same direction in all maps. In one adult map, the mean model correlation was above its control range, although the shared-site total was below its control mean. Thus fewer shared sites in total do not imply less average pair correlation. The controls omit local geometry. Finite randomization chains, selected cells and eight different animals limit inference. No activity or release failure was measured.

display.caption: Bilateral shared-site totals and mean pair correlations under a shared-event model. Gray marks show fixed-count control means and central 95 percent ranges. Blue marks show observed anatomy. These ranges are not animal confidence intervals.

citations.reason: We adapt its Curveball kernel and retrieval code. It tested recurrence of all target pairs. We test allocation to named bilateral partners.
We reuse its verified fixed panel and panel provenance. Its averaging model motivates the distinct bilateral allocation test.
